extracted.intended_audience: reading researchers, elementary educators, journalism educators, and literacy scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how typical newspaper narrative format, style, and content affect organization and comprehensibility for ordinary readers, with implications for reading development in children. Compares newspaper accounts with alternative narrative forms and discusses editorial style standards (sentence length, paragraphing, explicit relations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate format, style, and content for a news story
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' beliefs about the appropriate format, style, and content for a news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report argues these beliefs often 'work in concert to obscure the structure of the story and the relations among subparts' and thus may thwart the presumed goal of writing: 'providing an account of events that will be easily readable by an ordinary person.' Evaluate whether chosen format, style, and content clarify rather than obscure story structure and interrelations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of narrative structure and relations among subparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the story's overall organization and the relations among its subparts are explicit and perceptible to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author claims typical newspaper practice can obscure structure and subpart relations; assess if the narrative makes connections between events clear, supports comprehension of causal/temporal/semantic links, and signals organizational boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability for an ordinary person (comprehensibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the account of events is easily readable and understandable by an ordinary reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the presumed writing goal being evaluated. Consider sentence complexity, coherence, signposting of relations, and whether the text enables an ordinary reader to follow and integrate events without specialized knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence length (use of short sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of short sentences as an editorial/style standard (noted as common in texts aimed at beginning readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report notes editors' standards favor 'short sentences' for beginning-reader books; evaluate whether overly short sentences fragment information and impede readers' ability to perceive connections among ideas, especially in news narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraphing (presence or absence of paragraph breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the text uses paragraphing or presents text with little/no paragraph breaks (as observed in some editorial standards for beginning readers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report highlights 'no paragraphing' as a feature that may contribute to readers failing to learn to expect connections; assess whether paragraphing supports signaling of idea groupings and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness of relations between recounted events
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which relations among events (causal, temporal, explanatory, etc.) are made explicit in the narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report criticizes 'relations inexplicit between events recounted' as a problematic pattern; evaluate whether connective language and explicit cues are present to help readers form coherent representations of event relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of narrative form and alternative narrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of a typical newspaper account of an event with other possible ways of narrating the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether alternative narrative structures might better reveal organization and relations among ideas; consider if the chosen form serves comprehension goals or merely conforms to editorial conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implications for reading development (exposure effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: How exposure to texts conforming to certain editorial standards affects children's development as readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report hypothesizes that children exposed primarily to texts with short sentences, no paragraphing, and inexplicit relations 'may fail to become good readers because they do not learn to expect connection among ideas, and frequently fail to see it, even in better-written texts.' Evaluate texts with attention to long-term learning consequences for novice readers.
